evidence.claim: At Weir Farm, J. Alden Weir and his guests painted Ridgefield landscapes and the surrounding countryside.
evidence.quote: Weir and artists he hosted subsequently produced a large number of paintings depicting Ridgefield landscapes and other nearby countryside.

evidence.claim: J. Alden Weir acquired a 153-acre farm in Ridgefield in 1882, exchanging a painting and $10 for the property.
evidence.quote: in 1882 Weir settled instead on hilly countryside in the Branchville section of Ridgefield, acquiring a 153-acre farm there from Erwin Davis in exchange for $10 and a painting.

evidence.claim: His daughter Dorothy managed it after his death in 1919; after their 1931 marriage, her husband, sculptor Mahonri Young, built a second studio.
evidence.quote: Weir's daughter Dorothy Weir, a noted artist in her own right, took over management of the property following her father's death in 1919. Sculptor Mahonri Young would build a second studio at Weir Farm after the couple married in 1931.

evidence.claim: Preservation efforts followed a late-1980s subdivision of the farm for housing; the Trust for Public Land worked to reacquire the divided property.
evidence.quote: Prior to its permanent protection, Weir Farm had been subdivided for housing development in the late 1980s.  The Trust for Public Land worked to reacquire the divided land

evidence.claim: The property’s house and two artists’ studios underwent restoration and reopened to the public in May 2014.
evidence.quote: The two artist studios and house were restored to period, and in May 2014 were made accessible to the public again.
